title: Question everything
hook: Dominican schools teach through structured argument

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dominic's last promise to his weeping brothers: he'd be more useful after death. Your line was more useful then. Whose help did you name while using something they taught you? Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

It seems that God does not exist. That is how Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican friar and a saint, opens his own question on whether God exists, in the book he wrote to teach beginners about God. Before he gives a single argument for God, he lays out objections against. If God is all good, he asks, why is there evil? And if nature can explain things on its own, why do we need God at all? He states them fairly, in plain words, as if a sharp student had raised a hand. Only then does he answer. That way of thinking has a name, and Dominican schools taught by it. Today's word is the name.
screen: `IT SEEMS THAT GOD DOES NOT EXIST.` → `THE OBJECTIONS COME FIRST.` → `THEN THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: A disputation is a structured argument. In the universities where the friars taught, a master would set a question, students and other masters would raise objections, and then the master would weigh them and give an answer. The Summa of Thomas Aquinas is built like a disputation on paper, and its articles run in the same steps. First, the question: whether such and such is so. Second, the objections, each beginning, it seems that. Third, on the contrary: a voice from scripture or tradition on the other side. Fourth, I answer that: Thomas's own reasoning. And last, the replies, where he goes back to every objection, one by one, and answers it, often granting what's true in it. Notice what that does. You may not skip the hard question. You have to say the other side well enough that its friends would recognize it. And you have to answer every objection, not just the weak ones. For Dominicans, this is not doubt for its own sake. It rests on a conviction that truth can stand being questioned, that faith and reason aren't enemies. Paul puts the instinct in one short line, in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Test first, then hold on. At home, a disputation might look like this: before you dismiss the person you disagree with, say their best point out loud. Then answer that. A good question is the beginning of the answer.
screen: `A MASTER, A QUESTION, THE OBJECTIONS.` · `IT SEEMS THAT. ON THE CONTRARY.` · `I ANSWER THAT. THEN THE REPLIES.` · `TRUTH CAN STAND BEING QUESTIONED.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask one good question. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you believe firmly, about faith, about people, about anything. Now, gently, ask the question a sharp friend might ask against it. Don't answer yet. Just phrase it as fairly as you can, beginning the way Thomas does: it seems that. Hold the question in the quiet without flinching. Then notice what's true in it, even a little. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is, unfinished. The bell holds the time.
Disputation. A structured argument: the question, the objections stated fairly, the answer, and a reply to every objection. Today's word.
Your line: a good question. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's best point back to them before you make yours. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic seminaries and some university philosophy and theology courses still teach the Summa article by article, objections first, and some Dominican houses of study still argue questions out in structured debate.

The prologue says the Summa is for beginners (incipientes): the voice says 'to teach beginners about God'. Confirm. 'The great book' is descriptive, not a ranking; a Keeper may cut 'great'.
Description of the medieval disputation (master sets question, objections, master determines) is generalized; confirm.
